one_liner: Header-only C++11 small_vector, static_vector and small_flat_map that avoid heap allocation for up to N elements; no benchmark numbers.
what_it_does: sfl::small_vector<T, N, Allocator> follows the std::vector interface but keeps up to N elements in an inline array and switches to the allocator only beyond N; sfl::static_vector<T, N> never allocates and has a hard capacity of N; sfl::small_flat_map<Key, T, N> is a sorted-vector map stored in a small_vector. They are part of a larger family (vector, devector, segmented vectors, rb-tree, hash and flat maps and sets in plain, small_ and static_ variants) that meets the standard Container/AllocatorAwareContainer requirements, so code written against std::vector or std::map mostly compiles unchanged once the capacity parameter is added.
how_it_is_fast: The speed argument is allocation avoidance, not a new algorithm: small_vector holds three pointers (first, last, end of storage) plus a union of N elements, and the begin pointer always points at the live buffer, so element access and push_back are the same pointer arithmetic as std::vector with no inline-or-heap branch; growth is 1.5x and never drops below N. static_vector removes the allocator entirely (capacity is a compile-time constant and push_back only asserts it is not full). small_flat_map does a binary search (O(log n) lookup, O(n) insert/erase) over contiguous pairs, which is cache-friendly for small maps compared with node-based std::map.
when_to_use: Many short-lived vectors whose size is usually below a known bound (e.g. per-node child lists, argument lists, small result sets) where std::vector's first allocation dominates.
Bare-metal or allocation-free code paths that need a std::vector-shaped container with a fixed compile-time capacity (static_vector, also usable in C++20 constant expressions).
Small sorted maps (tens of keys) where a contiguous sorted array beats std::map's node allocations, and you want the inline-buffer variant of flat_map.
Codebases stuck on old toolchains: the library is tested down to GCC 4.8.5 and Clang 3.4.2 in C++11 mode, and supports stateful allocators and fancy pointers.
Teams that want one consistent family of small/static/flat containers from a single header-only, zlib-licensed project rather than mixing Boost, Abseil and LLVM types.
when_not_to_use: When you need evidence that it is faster: the project publishes no numbers for small_vector, static_vector or small_flat_map, and nothing compares it with boost::container::small_vector, absl::InlinedVector or llvm::SmallVector.

Memory-tight objects: the header layout gives 24 bytes of pointer overhead on 64-bit targets on top of N*sizeof(T) (derived from the header layout), where ankerl::svector and absl::InlinedVector document 8 bytes.

Large or frequently moved inline contents: moving or swapping a small_vector whose elements are inline moves element by element (documented as linear in N in the worst case), unlike std::vector's constant-time pointer swap.
Release builds that rely on capacity checks: static_vector overflow is only an assert (SFL_ASSERT is plain assert), so with NDEBUG an extra push_back writes past the inline array.
Constant-evaluated code using the small_* containers: the README says only non-small_* containers work in C++20 constant expressions.

integration.dependencies: none (standard library only); benchmarks additionally need Boost
integration.min_toolchain: C++11; tested GCC 4.8.5, Clang 3.4.2, GCC 7.3.1, Clang 5.0.1, GCC 15.2.1, Clang 22.1.1, MSVC 19.44 (C++14 and later); CMake 3.15+ for the INTERFACE target
integration.platforms: any with a conforming compiler (tested on CentOS 7 and Arch Linux x86-64 and MSVC; a 32-bit build problem, issue #29, was fixed in October 2025)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; no internal synchronization in the headers, so the usual std container rules apply by convention
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — std::vector-compatible member set (plus nth/index_of) with an extra capacity template parameter; moved-from objects are not guaranteed empty, static_vector has no allocator and UB on overflow, and small_flat_map's value_type is std::pair<Key, T> rather than std::pair<const Key, T>

gotchas: A moved-from small_vector may still hold its elements (documented 'valid but unspecified'); issue #3 (Dec 2023) was a user test asserting v1.size() == 0 after a move, closed by the maintainer as intended behavior. That reporter also said sfl::small_vector crashed in their program and switched to absl::InlinedVector, with no reproducer posted.
small_flat_map exposes std::pair<Key, T> with a non-const key through its iterators; modifying a key in place silently breaks the sort order the binary search relies on.

The record's 'many are constexpr in C++20' does not cover these entries' small_* types: the README states small_* containers are not usable in constant expressions; static_vector is, but on GCC you cannot declare a constexpr static_vector object and data() is not constexpr.

Benchmark harness (for other containers, not these three): benchmark/src/small_unordered_map.cpp and segmented_devector.cpp call std::mt19937 inside the timed loop for every element, and with 2-16 elements each sample is a single steady_clock interval; no results are checked in, so there is nothing to verify for small_vector, static_vector or small_flat_map.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick sfl when you want a standards-conforming, allocator-aware family (small_vector plus static, flat and linear-map variants) that builds on C++11 compilers and fancy pointers; pick ankerl::svector when you need published speedups and minimal 8-byte overhead, and ETL when you need a whole embedded, allocation-free container suite rather than just these types.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing was measured: the README and doc pages only call these containers 'compact and cache-friendly' and say small_vector avoids dynamic allocation for up to N elements; the repo's benchmark folder (g++ -std=c++20 -O3 -DNDEBUG makefile) times segmented_devector against std::deque and boost::container::deque and the hash maps against std::unordered_map, publishes no results, and has no harness for small_vector, static_vector or small_flat_map.
status_note: Actively maintained by a single author (886 commits, last on 2026-03-16 after a benchmark rework on 2026-03-10), zlib-licensed and header-only, so it is easy to vendor; tests are run under Valgrind, but treat its performance as unmeasured.
